# Exact obstruction to a low-maximum normal half-mass claim

The following tempting auxiliary claim is false: a positive simplex
normal with max_i u_i<=2/(d+1) need not put at least half the volume
on the positive side of the centroid. This does not contradict OC.

Take d=4, T=conv(0,e_1,e_2,e_3,e_4), and

    u=(2/5,2/5,1/10,1/10),       tau=1/5.

All coefficients are <=2/(d+1)=2/5 and sum to one. For X uniform
on T, write A=X_1+X_2 and B=X_3+X_4. The joint density on
{a>=0,b>=0,a+b<=1} is 24ab. This follows either by integrating the
two line-segment fibers directly or from the elementary Dirichlet
(2,2,1) density. Its integral over that triangle is one.

The cap u.X>=tau is equivalent to 4A+B>=2. It is empty for
a<1/3, has 2-4a<=b<=1-a for 1/3<=a<=1/2, and has
0<=b<=1-a for 1/2<=a<=1. Therefore its exact volume fraction is

    integral_(1/3)^(1/2) 12a[(1-a)^2-(2-4a)^2] da
      + integral_(1/2)^1 12a(1-a)^2 da
    = 73/432 + 5/16
    = 13/27 < 1/2.

The gap below half is 1/54. All integrations are finite polynomials,
and the cap boundary has zero four-dimensional volume. Thus any
argument for the remaining coefficient range must use information
beyond this proposed own-fiber median bound.
